evidence.claim: The Lower Susquehanna Scenic Byway links Perryville and Havre de Grace over 33 miles, climbing above Port Deposit and crossing the river atop Conowingo Dam.
evidence.quote: The Lower Susquehanna Scenic Byway comprises 33 miles (53 km) of highway between Havre de Grace and Perryville

evidence.claim: Maryland’s tourism office highlights river views, waterfront history and birding along this state scenic route, with a driving time of one to two hours.
evidence.quote: With sweeping river views, waterfront towns steeped in maritime history, and extraordinary birding, paddling and fishing spots

evidence.claim: with a driving time of one to two hours
evidence.quote: Drive time: 1-2 Hours

evidence.claim: On the western side, Susquehanna State Park brings heavy forest cover and large rock outcrops into the journey.
evidence.quote: Amid the heavy forest cover and massive rock outcrops of Susquehanna State Park

evidence.claim: The western route alternates between riverside Stafford Road and an inland stretch following Deer Creek, rather than tracing the bank throughout.
evidence.quote: At Deer Creek, the byway turns inland, following the creek then heading northwest toward Darlington.

evidence.claim: riverside Stafford Road
evidence.quote: Stafford Road, which parallels both the canal and the west bank of the river.

evidence.claim: The crossing changed when Conowingo Dam was built. Its reservoir would have submerged the existing U.S. Route 1 bridge, which was demolished in 1927; the highway now runs over the dam.
evidence.quote: The rising water also would have covered Conowingo Bridge, the original U.S. Route 1 crossing, so it was demolished in 1927. U.S. Route 1 now crosses over the top of the dam.

evidence.claim: The project also required the railroad to move to higher ground and displaced the original town of Conowingo.
evidence.quote: The dam's reservoir would flood a small town, the Columbia and Port Deposit Railroad mainline, and the existing Baltimore Pike bridge; all these needed to be relocated or replaced.

evidence.claim: the railroad to move to higher ground
evidence.quote: The railroad was relocated parallel at a higher elevation.

evidence.claim: The hydroelectric project was completed in 1928.
evidence.quote: When completed in 1928, it was the second-largest hydroelectric project

evidence.claim: From Perryville, head toward Port Deposit on the east bank, where older buildings occupy the narrow ground between river and bluffs.
evidence.quote: The bulk of the older buildings line the main street and the, until recently, single side street built in the narrow space between the bluffs and the river.

evidence.claim: Continue north to Conowingo Dam and cross on U.S. 1. On the west side, the byway reaches Susquehanna State Park before continuing to Havre de Grace.
evidence.quote: Rock Run Road leads to Susquehanna State Park.

evidence.claim: Continue north to Conowingo Dam
evidence.quote: Maryland Route 222 passes through the center of town along Main Street, connecting northwards to U.S. Route 1 near Conowingo Dam

evidence.claim: On the west side, the byway reaches Susquehanna State Park before continuing to Havre de Grace.
evidence.quote: The Lower Susquehanna Scenic Byway follows MD 155 (Level Road) west past I-95 to Webster Lapidum Road

evidence.claim: Finish beside the waterfront promenade and restored Concord Point Lighthouse.
evidence.quote: A half-mile-long waterfront promenade leads to the fully restored Concord Point Lighthouse .

evidence.claim: Port Deposit’s older buildings fit into a narrow strip between the Susquehanna and the bluffs, with terraces and stairs connecting streets above.
evidence.quote: The bulk of the older buildings line the main street and the, until recently, single side street built in the narrow space between the bluffs and the river. The bluffs have been terraced and stairways lead between streets.

evidence.claim: Its position once made it a transfer point: cargo coming downriver could be loaded onto Chesapeake ships here and at Lapidum, the northernmost navigable deepwater ports.
evidence.quote: This location, and Lapidum across the river, were the northernmost navigable deepwater ports on the Susquehanna.

evidence.claim: cargo coming downriver could be loaded onto Chesapeake ships
evidence.quote: where cargo could be transferred to ships from the Chesapeake.

evidence.claim: Local quarries supplied the stone commonly called Port Deposit granite, actually gneiss, used in many town buildings.
evidence.quote: A 4 acres (16,000 m2) site at the north end of Port Deposit was committed to quarrying "granite." (actually gneiss) for bridges.

evidence.claim: used in many town buildings
evidence.quote: This granite can be seen in many of the distinctive buildings in Port Deposit today.

evidence.claim: Many residences date to the early 1800s, part of the built waterfront encountered on the byway’s eastern side.
evidence.quote: On the east side of the river, Port Deposit features many residences that date to the early 1800s.

evidence.claim: From Main Street, a brick-and-stone staircase climbs 75 steps above town to a view of four river bridges.
evidence.quote: Accessible from Main Street, a brick-and-stone, 75-step staircase leads visitors above the town and allows a spectacular view of four bridges that cross the Susquehanna River.

evidence.claim: Look for the stone buildings and stairs rising between the riverfront streets and terraced bluffs.
evidence.quote: The bluffs have been terraced and stairways lead between streets.

evidence.claim: Look for the stone buildings
evidence.quote: The town has several impressive older buildings, many built of the local granite or brick.

evidence.claim: U.S. 1 crosses the top of Conowingo Dam, replacing a bridge demolished before the reservoir filled.
evidence.quote: The rising water also would have covered Conowingo Bridge, the original U.S. Route 1 crossing, so it was demolished in 1927. U.S. Route 1 now crosses over the top of the dam.

evidence.claim: Philadelphia Electric Company commissioned the project; Stone & Webster designed it, and Maryland’s Arundel Corporation carried out construction beginning in 1926.
evidence.quote: On January 23, 1925, Philadelphia Electric Company awarded the construction contract for the dam to Stone & Webster of Boston, who did the design.  Construction, which started in 1926, was carried out by the Arundel Corporation of Maryland.

evidence.claim: The reservoir covers the original town of Conowingo, which was moved during construction. The dam was completed in 1928.
evidence.quote: The dam supports a 9,000-acre reservoir, which today covers the original town of Conowingo. During dam construction, the town was moved to its present location

evidence.claim: The dam was completed in 1928.
evidence.quote: When completed in 1928

evidence.claim: Construction reshaped the transport corridor as well as the river: the Columbia and Port Deposit Railroad was moved to a higher elevation.
evidence.quote: The railroad was relocated parallel at a higher elevation.

evidence.claim: the Columbia and Port Deposit Railroad was moved
evidence.quote: the Columbia and Port Deposit Railroad mainline

evidence.claim: At Fisherman’s Wharf & Park, hawks, great blue herons and bald eagles are often seen along the river.
evidence.quote: Hawks, great blue herons and bald eagles are often spied from Fisherman's Wharf & Park at Conowingo Dam

evidence.claim: The waterfront promenade leads to Concord Point Lighthouse where the Susquehanna meets the Chesapeake Bay.
evidence.quote: A half-mile-long waterfront promenade leads to the fully restored Concord Point Lighthouse .

evidence.claim: where the Susquehanna meets the Chesapeake Bay
evidence.quote: It is situated at the mouth of the Susquehanna River and the head of the Chesapeake Bay.

evidence.claim: Hurricane Isabel destroyed the promenade in September 2003. It was rebuilt in 2004 with help from AmeriCorps NCCC and again connects Tydings Park, the Maritime Museum and the lighthouse.
evidence.quote: In September 2003, Hurricane Isabel flooded the city about two blocks into downtown, destroying the promenade. It was rebuilt in 2004, with help from Americorps NCCC.

evidence.claim: again connects Tydings Park, the Maritime Museum and the lighthouse
evidence.quote: Today, it serves as a waterfront boardwalk and nature walk from Tydings Park to the Maritime Museum, and on to Concord Point Lighthouse.

evidence.claim: Elsewhere on the waterfront, the restored lock house preserves another transport story. Havre de Grace was the southern end of the Susquehanna and Tidewater Canal, built to bypass difficult river navigation between here and Wrightsville, Pennsylvania.
evidence.quote: This was built to bypass difficult navigational areas of the lower Susquehanna River between Havre de Grace and Wrightsville, Pennsylvania

evidence.claim: the restored lock house
evidence.quote: is located in a restored lock house.

evidence.claim: Havre de Grace was the southern end of the Susquehanna and Tidewater Canal
evidence.quote: The town was the southern terminus for the Proprietors of the Susquehanna Canal and later the Susquehanna and Tidewater Canal.

evidence.claim: The lock keeper’s house and canal remnants form a museum.
evidence.quote: The Lock Keeper's house and remnants of the canal exist today as a museum.

flags: Dropped current Havre de Grace claims about losing the national capital by one vote and hereditary lighthouse keepers appointed by the town. They occur in the encyclopedic town page, but the cache contains no suitable corroborating historical record; retained the lighthouse through its documented waterfront setting.
A construction chronology is not available for the entire byway. Used documented U.S. 1 bridge replacement and dam construction as the road history; no byway designation date claimed.
The Port Deposit page gives 1927 for the dam; the dedicated dam page distinguishes 1927 bridge demolition from 1928 project completion. Used the dedicated chronology.

Used the tourism office’s 33-mile corridor rather than material’s 30 mapped miles. Strip places put Lapidum at mile 2.17 despite its west-bank location; retained moments follow the consistent Perryville–Port Deposit–dam–Havre de Grace sequence.
Port Deposit’s canal paragraph conflates canals and banks. Avoided its canal chronology; used only supported deepwater-transfer history and local stone.
Tourism page still describes Steppingstone’s display barn; the dedicated museum page records its destruction in June 2024. Did not suggest that barn survives or can be visited.
No material motifs were adopted; current river-bluffs and lighthouse motifs are retained. Omitted “33 miles around” to avoid implying a closed driving loop.
